name: The two kinds of memory and the theory of perception
plain_explanation: Bergson distinguishes memory as mere habit (like reciting a poem from repeated practice) from memory as recollection of a unique, dated past event; he argues the second kind cannot be a function of the brain at all, and that at the opposite extreme, 'pure perception' is really part of matter itself.
precise_definition: In Matter and Memory, Bergson holds that 'the past survives... under two distinct forms: first, in motor mechanisms; secondly, in independent recollections,' arguing that true (recollective) memory is 'a power absolutely independent of matter,' while 'pure perception,' at the opposite pole, is 'the lowest degree of mind... really part of matter,' with the brain's function being merely to select, for practical action, from an otherwise limitless field of potential perception.
why_it_mattered: It is Bergson's proposed solution to the mind-matter relation, and the empirical basis (via brain physiology and amnesia) on which he argues that memory, and therefore mind, cannot be reduced to matter.
historical_origin: Set out in Matter and Memory.
examples: The distinction between reciting a memorized poem by habit versus recollecting the specific, dated occasions on which one read it
objections: Russell traces Bergson's key term 'image' -- defined as something 'placed half-way between the thing and the representation' -- to a persistent, unresolved confusion between the mental act of imaging and the object imaged
